verdict.rationale: The command to sing praise to God is lexically unambiguous and spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical). Psalm 100:1-2 stacks three direct orders (H7321 'shout', H5647+H8057 'serve with gladness', H0935+H7445 'come with ringing song'), and Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 hang the participles 'sing' (ado, G0103) and 'make melody' (psallo, G5567) on the governing commands 'be filled' (pleroustho, Ephesians 5:18) and 'let it dwell' (enoiketo, Colossians 3:16). Additional New Testament verbs 'hymn' (hymneo, G5214) at Matthew 26:30, Mark 14:26, Acts 16:25 and Hebrews 2:12, and the 'each one has a psalm' construction at 1 Corinthians 14:26 ('each one has a psalm', ekastos psalmon echei), confirm congregational sung praise as commanded New Testament practice. What the lexical pattern does NOT settle is the scope claim embedded in the proposition. The three nouns 'psalm' (psalmos, G5568), 'hymn' (hymnos, G5215), and 'song' (ode, G5603) all attach to canonical psalms in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint): 'psalm' (psalmos) and 'song' (ode) as Psalter superscriptions; 'hymn' (hymnos) at Psalm 72:20 in the Septuagint. The triad of three can be read either as three labels for the inspired Psalter, or as three distinct genres one of which ('hymn', hymnos) is non-Psalter composition. The morphology (word-form analysis) and Greek lexicon alone do not adjudicate. Hence the verdict 'affirms' is 'disputed' on the precise proposition as worded, while the singing core is affirmed.

scripture.force: Three datives (nouns in the 'to/with/by-X' grammatical form) 'to/with psalms' (psalmois), 'hymns' (hymnois), and 'spiritual songs' (odais pneumatikais) stand in series as the means of mutual address 'speaking to one another' (laloontes heautois), with the participles 'singing' (ado) and 'making melody' (psallo) dependent on the prior command in verse 18 'be filled with the Spirit' (pleroustho en pneumati). The force is hortatory (urging, exhorting): congregational singing is enjoined. The adjective 'spiritual' (pneumatikais) is morphologically (in its word-form) feminine plural and so attaches grammatically only to 'songs' (odais, also feminine), although by sense it can govern the whole triad of three. The three nouns themselves are not lexically defined in context, so whether they mark three distinct genres or three Psalter labels is left open by the syntax (sentence structure).

The governing command 'let dwell' (enoiketo, 'let the word of Christ dwell richly', plousios) is filled out by the participles 'teaching' (didasko) and 'admonishing' (noutheteo), with 'to/with psalms' (psalmois), 'hymns' (hymnois), and 'spiritual songs' (odais pneumatikais) as the dative (instrumental, 'by-means-of') instrument of that mutual teaching and admonishing, capped by 'singing in grace in your hearts to God' (ado en te chariti en tais kardiais hymon to theo). The didactic (teaching-related) verbs tie sung praise to instruction, which suits content of real doctrinal weight. As in Ephesians the three nouns are listed without lexical definition, and the parallel construction reinforces both readings (a Psalter triad of three vs three genres).

The opening command 'make a joyful shout' (hariu, H7321 in the hiphil, the Hebrew causative form 'to cause to shout', as a command) is addressed to all the earth ('all the earth', kol haarets), with the superscription 'a psalm for thanksgiving' (mizmor letodah) framing the whole. The verbal command to vocal praise is direct and universal in address, establishing the Old Testament command-to-sing baseline that the New Testament participles in Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 inherit.

Three commands: 'serve YHWH with gladness' (ivdu et YHWH besimcha), 'come before him with ringing song' (bou lefanav birnanah). The pairing of joyful corporate service with sung approach shows worship-song as enjoined corporate response, reinforcing that singing praise is commanded, not merely permitted.

When you come together 'each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation' (hekastos psalmon echei, didachen echei, apokalypsin echei). The verb 'has' (echei, G2192 present active, an ongoing simple statement of fact) with 'each one' (hekastos) describes individual contributions brought to the assembly; 'psalm' (psalmos) here stands alongside teaching and revelation as something one brings, which on the surface reads more naturally as a contributed sung composition than as a recitation of a Psalter text. This is the strongest New Testament lexical datum that 'psalm' (psalmos) in the New Testament vocabulary can name something composed, not solely a canonical Psalm.

'And having hymned they went out to the Mount of Olives' (Kai hymnesantes exelthon eis to oros ton elaion). The aorist participle (a completed past action in participle form) of 'hymn' (hymneo, G5214) names the Last Supper sung praise. The verb cognate to 'hymn' (hymnos, G5215) is used here without specifying content, but the Passover liturgical setting makes the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113-118) the natural referent. The verse documents New Testament congregational hymning as a fact of Jesus' own practice.

'Paul and Silas praying were hymning God' (Paulos kai Silas proseuchomenoi hymnoun ton theon). The imperfect tense (ongoing or repeated past action) of 'hymn' (hymneo, G5214) describes sustained sung praise by two New Testament apostles in prison. The content is not specified; the practice is recorded as ordinary New Testament worship.

'Is anyone cheerful? Let them make melody / sing-psalm' (Euthumei tis? psalleto). The third-person singular command of 'make melody / sing' (psallo, G5567) is the New Testament command that pairs joy with sung response, parallel to Ephesians 5:19 'making melody' (psallontes). The verb's range covers both 'play a stringed instrument' and 'sing a psalm', and the absence of a specified object leaves content underdetermined.

'They sing a new song' (Adousin oden kainen). The collocation of 'sing' (ado) and 'song' (ode) with 'new' (kainos) picks up the Old Testament pattern 'sing to YHWH a new song' (shiru lYHWH shir chadash) at Psalm 33:3, Psalm 96:1, Psalm 98:1, Psalm 149:1, and Isaiah 42:10. The heavenly song is sung with explicit content ('worthy is the Lamb'), so in the New Testament use 'song' (ode) is not restricted to the Old Testament Psalter; a 'new song' is composed and sung in response to the slain Lamb. This is decisive lexical evidence that 'song' (ode, G5603) in New Testament use names sung praise that is not coextensive (does not overlap entirely) with the canonical Psalter.

'In the midst of the congregation I will hymn you' (En meso ekklesias hymneso se). Hebrews 2:12 quotes Psalm 22:22 from the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), putting 'hymn' (hymneo, G5214) on the lips of Christ as the leader of congregational praise. This both grounds New Testament hymning in the Psalter and connects the verb 'hymn' (hymneo) to ecclesial (church-assembly) sung praise as Christological (Christ-centered) practice.

complicating_texts.resolution: The same verse that commands congregational singing is the chief proof-text for the exclusive-psalmody (Psalms-only-singing) minority reading. Because 'psalm' (psalmos), 'hymn' (hymnos), and 'song' (ode) all attach to canonical psalms in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint): 'psalm' (psalmos) in superscriptions like Psalm 3, Psalm 4, Psalm 5; 'song' (ode) in Psalm 4, Psalm 18, Psalm 30; 'hymn' (hymnos) at Psalm 72:20 in the Septuagint, the threefold list can be read as a triple designation of the inspired Psalter rather than as three distinct genres. Lexical data permits both the inclusive reading (three categories, only one of which is the Psalter) and the restrictive reading (three Psalter labels). The matter is not dissolved at the morphology (word-form analysis) layer.

Parallel to Ephesians, the identical three-noun series with 'spiritual' (pneumatikais) governs the dispute. The didactic (teaching-related) verbs 'teach' (didasko, G1321) and 'admonish' (noutheteo, G3560) establish that sung content carries doctrinal instruction, which one reading takes as favoring richly composed hymns and the other reading takes as describing the canonical Psalter teaching the church. The morphology (word-form analysis) and lexicon do not adjudicate.

'Each one has a psalm' (ekastos psalmon echei) construes 'psalm' (psalmos) as something individually brought, which weighs against the restrictive Psalter-only reading of the noun. However, exclusive-psalmody (Psalms-only-singing) advocates respond that 'has a psalm' could still mean 'has a psalm to offer from the Psalter' (i.e. has memorized and presents). The construction reduces but does not eliminate the ambiguity in the New Testament use of 'psalm' (psalmos).

'They sing a new song' (Adousin oden kainen) with specified non-Psalter content is the strongest lexical argument that 'song' (ode, G5603) in New Testament use is not coextensive (does not overlap entirely) with the canonical Psalter. The minority response is that Revelation 5:9 records a heavenly, eschatological (end-times) song that does not licence congregational composition in time. The lexical pattern itself favors the inclusive reading but does not, by morphology (word-form analysis) alone, settle whether earthly congregational use of non-Psalter 'song' (ode) is commanded.

variants.note: The supplied bundle lists no variant units for Ephesians 5:19, Colossians 3:16, Psalm 100:1-2. The SBLGNT (the SBL Greek New Testament) apparatus marks on Ephesians 5:19 (the precise placement of 'spiritual', pneumatikais) and Colossians 3:16 ('in', en vs no 'in', en, before 'psalms', psalmois; 'to God', theo vs 'to the Lord', kyrio at clause close) touch arrangement of vocabulary, not the presence of the three song-nouns. No plausible variant reading would change the verdict on the singing core or on the scope question. The ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) is not in scope for these books outside 3 John.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: 'Psalm' (psalmos, G5568), 'hymn' (hymnos, G5215), and 'song' (ode, G5603) are read as three Greek-Old-Testament (Septuagint) titles for canonical psalms, so the Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 triad of three commands singing the inspired Psalter and warrants no non-canonical hymn. On this lens the proposition as worded, which expressly includes composed historic hymns and modern songs, is denied. The strongest lexical support for this reading is that all three Greek nouns appear in Greek-Old-Testament (Septuagint) Psalm superscriptions, and 'spiritual' (pneumatikais, G4152) is read as 'inspired' (i.e. canonically Spirit-given), restricting the triad of three to inspired Psalter song.

The three nouns mark genuinely distinct genres; 'song' (ode) in New Testament use (Revelation 5:9, Revelation 14:3, Revelation 15:3 paired with 'new', kainos) is not coextensive (does not overlap entirely) with the Psalter, and 1 Corinthians 14:26 ('each one has a psalm', ekastos psalmon echei) treats 'psalm' (psalmos) as an individually contributed item. The didactic (teaching-related) verbs 'teach' (didasko) and 'admonish' (noutheteo) in Colossians 3:16 invite Spirit-shaped composed praise. 'Hymn' (hymneo, G5214) at Matthew 26:30, Acts 16:25, Hebrews 2:12 records New Testament sung praise as ordinary practice. So doctrinally rich hymns and biblically grounded songs are licensed, and congregational singing is commanded.

Stripped of the scope dispute, both testaments command congregational sung praise: Psalm 100:1-2 Old Testament commands 'shout' (hariu), 'serve' (ivdu), 'come' (bou); Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 New Testament participles 'sing' (ado) and 'make melody' (psallo) under the governing commands 'be filled' (pleroustho) and 'let dwell' (enoiketo); James 5:13 'let him make melody' (psalleto) as direct command; 'hymn' (hymneo, G5214) at Matthew 26:30, Mark 14:26, Acts 16:25, Hebrews 2:12 as descriptive of New Testament sung praise. The act of singing praise to God is good and commanded on any defensible reading of the words.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns not on whether singing is commanded (it plainly is, Old Testament and New Testament) but on the scope of admissible song content. The lexical pattern is genuinely contested at the scope layer. Both lenses preserve the singing command; they diverge only on whether the triad of three nouns includes non-Psalter composition.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What kinds of sung material does Scripture command for the gathered people of God, and do the New Testament terms 'psalm' (psalmos, G5568), 'hymn' (hymnos, G5215), and 'song' (ode, G5603) denote three distinct genres or three designations of the canonical Psalter?
stem_audit.notes: The original stem bundles an uncontested claim (singing praise to God is good and commanded) with a contested scope claim (that composed historic hymns and modern songs are among what is commanded). The parenthetical pre-decides the exclusive-psalmody (Psalms-only-singing) dispute in favor of inclusion. The verdict is derived on the original stem, which is why 'affirms' is 'disputed' rather than 'true': the command core is affirmed but the embedded scope verdict is lexically open.

lay_summary: The words behind this question are plain that singing praise to God is commanded, and that command runs through the whole Bible. In Psalm 100 the verbs are direct orders: make a joyful shout, serve with gladness, come before him with ringing song. In Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 the acts of singing ('sing', ado) and making melody ('make melody', psallo) hang on the governing commands to be filled with the Spirit and to let the word of Christ dwell richly, so congregational singing is enjoined, not merely allowed. The teaching and admonishing verbs in Colossians tie sung praise to instruction, which fits content of real doctrinal weight. James 5:13 puts the command directly: if anyone is cheerful, let them sing-psalm (psallo). Matthew 26:30 and Acts 16:25 record Jesus with the Twelve, and Paul with Silas, actually hymning ('hymn', hymneo). Where the words stop short is the precise scope of what may be sung. Both Ephesians and Colossians list the same three nouns: 'psalm' (psalmos), 'hymn' (hymnos), and 'spiritual song' (pneumatikos ode). In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) all three of these words attach to canonical psalms, so the threefold list can be read two ways. One reading takes them as three labels for the inspired Psalter, which would limit sung worship to the Book of Psalms. The other reading takes them as three distinct kinds of song, one of which is freshly composed praise, which would licence rich hymns and biblically grounded songs. Two New Testament data points push toward the second reading without finally settling it: in 1 Corinthians 14:26 each person in the assembly is said to have a 'psalm' (psalmos) as something brought (like a teaching or a revelation), and in Revelation 5:9 the heavenly company sings a new 'song' (ode) with non-Psalter content (worthy is the Lamb). But the minority reading has answers to both. The morphology (word-form analysis), the lexicon, and the cross-references do not by themselves decide. So the act of singing praise is affirmed without reservation, while the specific claim that composed hymns and modern songs are among what is commanded is left genuinely open by the words alone. That is why the overall verdict on this proposition, as it is worded, is recorded as contested rather than settled.
